newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada settles former PM Mulroney's libel suit.
newsitem.headline: Canada settles former PM Mulroney's libel suit.

text.p: The Canadian government has apologized to former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney over allegations he received kickbacks on an airplane deal, avoiding an unprecedented C$50 million ($37 million) libel lawsuit, his lawyers said on Monday.

In an out-of-court settlement reached on Sunday, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) agreed to pay Mulroney's legal costs, which were undisclosed, while the former prime minister agreed to waive his claim to damages.

The government apologized for wrongly accusing Mulroney of taking kickbacks in Air Canada's C$1.8 billion ($1.3 billion) purchase of Airbus jets in 1988. Mulroney's lawyers gave details of the settlement in a Montreal court where the libel suit was to have begun on Monday.

The settlement included an acknowledgement by the RCMP that any conclusions of wrongdoing by Mulroney "were -- and are -- unjustified." "The government of Canada and the RCMP regret any damage suffered by Mr. Mulroney and his family and fully apologize to them," it said.

Mulroney, Canada's Conservative prime minister from 1984 to 1993, sued the Justice Department and RCMP in November 1995 over allegations in an official letter they sent to Swiss authorities in September 1995 accusing him of accepting illegal commissions in the Airbus purchase.

Air Canada, now a publicly held company, was owned by the government when it bought the 34 Airbus A-320 jets in 1988. The Justice Department letter said Mulroney was suspected of accepting up to C$4 million ($3 million) in kickbacks in the deal and of being part of a "conspiracy" with former Newfoundland Premier Frank Moores and businessman Karlheinz Schreiber to defraud the Canadian government.

At a news conference, his lawyers said the settlement exonerated Mulroney of any wrongdoing in the Airbus matter. "Mr. Mulroney's name has been vindicated and that is the only thing he really wanted," Gerald Tremblay told reporters.

Tremblay said Mulroney agreed to the last-minute settlement because it included an unequivocal apology and recognition by the government that the 31 allegations against him in the 11-page Justice Department letter were groundless.

Until it agreed to that apology, the government had been willing only to express regret that the letter, which asked Swiss authorities to obtain information on certain bank accounts in Switzerland, had been leaked to the media.

Tremblay said Mulroney, a corporate lawyer who led the Tories to victories in the 1984 and 1988 federal elections, was pleased with the settlement. "Mr. Mulroney is back at work and very happy to continue on with his life," he said.
Government officials said they were satisfied with the settlement but the RCMP refused to say whether Mulroney would no longer be part of its ongoing investigation of the Airbus deal.
"I'm not saying Mr. Mulroney is or isn't a suspect," RCMP Commissioner Philip Murray told a news conference in Ottawa.

Allan Rock, the Liberal government's justice minister, said the agreement was in the "best interests" of the government, the justice system and taxpayers, but he also did not rule out further investigation of Mulroney. "This agreement does not stop the RCMP's ongoing criminal investigation into Airbus, or give anyone, including Mr. Mulroney, effective immunity from such an investigation," Rock said.

The libel suit, unprecedented for its scope, could have had profound legal and political implications if it had gone to trial. Mulroney's lawyers had subpoenaed several senior government officials including Rock.
In the settlement, the parties agreed Rock was not involved in the RCMP's decision to initiate the Airbus investigation.
